chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Sayf, from his father Sayf, from Abdul A'la ibn Ayn, who said:

Some of our companions wrote, asking Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about certain matters, and instructed me to ask him about the right of the Muslim upon his brother. So I asked him, but he did not answer me. When I came to bid him farewell, I said, 'I asked you, but you did not answer me.' He said, 'I fear that you will be disbelieving. Indeed, among the most difficult of what Allah has imposed upon His creatures are three: The fairness of a man towards himself, until he is pleased for his brother from himself only with what he is pleased for his own self from him; and the sharing of wealth with the brother; and the remembrance of Allah in every state—not merely saying 'Glory be to Allah' and 'Praise be to Allah', but when Allah prohibits something for him, he leaves it.'

key_terms.إِنْصَافَ الْمَرْءِ مِنْ نَفْسِهِ: Fairness of the man from himself
key_terms.حَقِّ الْمُسْلِمِ عَلَى أَخِيهِ: Right of the Muslim upon his brother
key_terms.ذِكْرَ اللَّهِ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ: Remembrance of Allah in every state

ai.seo_question: What are the three most difficult rights of the Muslim upon his brother according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) reveals that these three rights are among the most difficult obligations because they require internalizing justice and constant mindfulness beyond mere ritual. The emphasis on 'self-fairness' (insaf al-nafs) aligns with the Shia concept of *nafs* purification, while linking remembrance (*dhikr*) to abstaining from prohibitions reflects the Quranic principle that true piety is measured by avoiding sin. This hadith serves as a practical guide for believers to integrate spiritual consciousness into daily social and financial interactions.
